sections.title: Why I wanted to build an AI civilization sandbox
sections.body:
These are screenshots from the running game, using manually staged scenarios to show different parts of the experience. They are not an autonomous AI playthrough. The images retain the original Chinese UI; select one to view it at full size.

01 / THE WORLD

If several AIs developed on the same continent, how would they choose their paths? That is the question I most wanted to explore with Civilization Z. I gave three civilizations a default 24 × 18 hex map and a capital each, with fog to explore, cities to establish and resources to gather. They act in sequence before a shared settlement phase, with a default limit of 60 rounds.

What interests me is how those choices change the map: where a city goes, how resources are split between research and expansion, and when to prepare for conflict. I kept a free offline rule-based strategy so the game can run without an API; it does not call a language model. Connecting DeepSeek → Jev lets me observe model decisions under the same rules. For now, it is a single-player sandbox running in a local browser.

sections.title: Making city development a choice
sections.body:
02 / CITY BUILDING

I wanted a city to need attention after it was founded. Population, food and production set its pace; granaries, workshops, libraries and new units take multiple rounds. Build another settler first, or invest in a library? Limited production time gives that choice weight.

Research, industry and military specializations give cities different roles, alongside limited construction investment. I also kept direct controls: during a takeover, players can select a city to arrange production or a unit to set a destination and inspect attack risks. Natural language is useful for expressing intent, but it should not be required for every move.

sections.title: Leaving room for different paths
sections.body:
03 / VICTORY PATHS

Victory conditions give development a purpose. I set up two ways to finish early: a science victory requires Scientific Method followed by its research project; conquest requires control of every initial capital at once. If neither happens before the round limit, the game is decided by a combined score.

I want these routes to pull against one another. Research depends on city output, expansion requires construction, and preparing for war uses resources too. Shared limits on time and resources let an immediate choice shape the later game. Giving each route a fair chance is still part of the balancing work ahead.

sections.title: Taking part without having to take over
sections.body:
04 / PLAYER AGENCY

When AI simply keeps playing, it can be hard to tell why it stopped or what it is working toward. I added map action bubbles, a location-aware chronicle and public goals to make spectating easier to follow. Intentions stay separate from results. Viewers can follow a civilization or region and pause automatically at events such as a declaration of war or an attack on a capital.

I split participation into two levels. A lighter intervention gives a civilization direction for five AI decisions, such as prioritizing research or defending territory, while leaving individual moves to it. For direct control, players can take over at its next eligible action phase. Leaving ends that phase, with AI returning in the following round.

sections.title: Letting the map tell the story
sections.body:
05 / ON THE MAP

I would rather a viewer remember a fight at a mountain pass or a city changing hands than another few lines in a log. Units move under terrain, movement and occupancy rules; the engine resolves attacks and counterattacks. The interface then turns those events into paths, damage numbers and bubbles. Even a long march has visible progress on the map.

I chose miniature cities, hand-painted terrain and an antique-map palette, with city art changing as population grows. Drawers open only when needed, leaving most of the screen to the world. Resource and military overlays, labels and text sizing are adjustable. Rather than display everything at once, I want the current situation to be readable at a glance.

sections.title: Connecting model decisions to a rule engine
sections.body:
06 / THE DECISION PIPELINE

The engineering separation I care most about is between a model expressing intent and the game changing state. TypeScript workspaces hold the rule engine, AI adapter, shared contracts, Fastify server and React frontend. Model decisions follow the four stages below. The offline strategy produces candidate commands directly, but uses the same rule validation.

  1. 01 / OBSERVE

    Scoped observation

    Each civilization receives its own state, visible map and private memory. Spectators can see the whole world; a model decides from its civilization's perspective.

  2. 02 / TRANSLATE

    Strategy & translation

    DeepSeek proposes actions and Jev translates them into structured commands tied to source text spans. Plans, quotations and unresolved text are not executed directly.

  3. 03 / VALIDATE

    Server adjudication

    The server checks the run, state version and control authority. The rule engine then validates commands and resolves movement, construction and combat.

  4. 04 / RECORD

    Facts & feedback

    Execution results become events that drive the map, chronicle and next observation. Blocked actions retain their reasons for explanation and debugging.

Human natural-language commands also go through preview, confirmation and execution. Loading a save creates a new runtime instance so old requests cannot change the restored world. Model budgets are tracked separately, and loading an earlier save does not reset consumed calls. These are quiet details, but they matter when pause, takeover and saving need to work together reliably.

I kept pause, single-step and speed controls in the viewing experience. Sometimes I just want to watch development; sometimes I want to stop and understand one decision. Saves let a game continue, while the chronicle recalls key events. A full replay of model responses is not implemented yet; that is a different problem from restoring a game.

sections.title: Next, I want to make each game worth following
sections.body:
07 / CURRENT STATE

Around the core game, I added a main menu, an opening film, background music and a five-step offline tutorial, plus two fixed challenges: defending a capital and bringing a trailing civilization back into contention. I want a first-time player to know where to start without first learning the model configuration or a long list of rules.

My next focus is the pace of a whole game: whether the early development phase stays interesting, whether war and research both offer opportunities, and whether the later rounds still have decisions worth stepping into. Finishing a game is the baseline. I want it to let me observe AI decisions and give someone a reason to watch the next round.

For now, I am continuing it as a local single-player project; I have not opened a public online demo or released the source. Offline play has no model-call costs. Real-model play and natural-language translation require provider configuration and involve API costs.

projects.title: Trading Simulator
projects.tag: Native macOS · Market Engine · Simulation Game
projects.lede: Stock Market Rookie Village is a native macOS trading simulation game that combines deterministic market generation, A-share-style rules, event-driven prices, and challenge scoring into a replayable local experience.
images: Stock Market Rookie Village native macOS trading simulator
Stock Market Rookie Village native macOS trading simulator

sections.title: A Credible Decision Environment Without Live Market Data
sections.body:
Overview

The project separates presentation, market generation, and trade settlement. The native SwiftUI app provides the multi-window terminal, while the Fastify backend owns authoritative quotes, positions, fees, events, challenges, and saves. SQLite persists the complete state of each game.

Players can advance the market freely in sandbox mode or enter fixed-day challenges that balance asset targets, maximum drawdown, and trade count. Every stock, price, news item, and event is fictional.

sections.title: Market Prices Emerge from Multiple Interacting Factors
sections.body:
Market Simulation

Each save stores its own market seed, regime, and difficulty snapshot. Price generation combines market sentiment, capital style, volume heat, sector rotation, stock volatility, event impact, and event-chain persistence, while applying 10% or 20% price-limit boundaries by board.

Market Regime

03 / EVENT
Event Driver
Market, industry, and stock events carry direction, strength, and duration, including chains and expectation reversals.

sections.title: Custom Multi-Period K-Lines for a Desktop Terminal
sections.body:
Native Charting

The K-line chart is drawn with SwiftUI Canvas and supports 1, 5, 15, 30, and 60-minute periods plus daily, weekly, and monthly views. Candles, MA5 / MA10 / MA20, volume, volume averages, price and time axes, the latest-price line, and crosshair readings are rendered together.

One-minute data only exposes bars reached by the simulation clock. Other intraday periods aggregate visible minute bars, while weekly and monthly views aggregate daily bars. Players can switch among 30, 45, and 60-bar ranges with pan, zoom, and playback controls.

sections.title: Server-Authoritative Rules and Multi-Window Consistency
sections.body:
Trading Integrity

The trading engine enforces 100-share lots, T+1, cash and sellable-position checks, commissions, stamp duty, and price-limit direction rules. SQLite transactions update accounts, positions, and trades together before recalculating market value, total assets, returns, and maximum drawdown.

Every order carries an idempotency key, so retries return the existing trade. Writes also verify expectedStateVersion, preventing stale windows from overwriting newer game state. The main terminal and separate position, order, and chart windows therefore share one authoritative state.

sections.title: Comparable Strategy Challenges Across Market Regimes
sections.body:
Challenge & Saves

The game includes 20-day warm-up, 60-day beginner, and 120-day steady-growth challenges. Settlement combines asset targets, maximum drawdown, and minimum trade count into a score and S, A, B, or C rating. Difficulty adjusts challenge targets, while sandbox mode has no forced ending.

Multiple saves can be created, loaded, renamed, and deleted. The same content pack generates different market paths under different seeds, regimes, and difficulties while keeping each save reproducible for continued play and verification.

sections.title: Native Terminal, Domain Engine, and Maintainable Content Packs
sections.body:
Architecture & Content

The native app's ObservableObject Store connects to the Fastify API. The backend domain layer owns market, order, portfolio, event, challenge, and save logic before persisting to local SQLite. The older React frontend remains a debugging surface rather than the default product.

Industries, stocks, market regimes, difficulties, and event templates live in CSV content packs. Startup validation checks headers, unique IDs, industry references, enum values, and minimum counts so content can expand without changing core trading code.

Native Multi-Window UI
Terminal, chart, positions, orders, news, events, and saves share state across windows.
02
Multi-Period Market Data
Intraday, daily, weekly, and monthly K-lines follow consistent price and volume constraints.
03
Event Chains
Fictional news affects markets, industries, and stocks, then decays or reverses over trading days.
04
Trade Consistency
Transactions, idempotency keys, and state versions protect accounts and multi-window actions.
05
Challenge Scoring
Scores combine returns, drawdown, and trading completion rather than final assets alone.
06
Local Saves
Game data stays in local SQLite without collecting real identity information.
This project is for gaming and learning only. It does not connect to live market data, real trading, or brokerage accounts, and it provides no investment advice or return promises.

sections.title: Beyond Booking: Support the Daily Work of a Venue
sections.body:
Overview

BF Badminton starts with a shared court schedule for online and walk-in service, connecting member accounts, payment orders, stock, pickup credentials, events and community features. Customers book and purchase; front-desk staff handle walk-ins, top-ups and collection; administrators manage operations and permissions; maintenance staff have read-only access to maintenance schedules.

The frontend uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Pinia, and Element Plus. The backend uses Tornado's asynchronous request model with an aiomysql pool and asynchronous Redis client for network and database I/O.

Screenshots captured on 2026-09-29 show the local isolated demo, with the original Chinese interface; most historical transactions date to September 24. Payment is an in-project simulation, not the official Alipay sandbox or a real transfer. Production HTTPS deployment, WeChat public-account linking and physical scanning devices require separate acceptance. Select an image to open its original.

sections.title: Protect Court Use and Payments with Transactions, Row Locks and Idempotency
sections.body:
Concurrency Control

New bookings now use MySQL transactions as the authoritative boundary. FOR UPDATE locks the relevant court rows before checking active bookings, maintenance blocks and confirmed prices; reservations, payment orders and audit records commit together. Online booking, walk-ins, extensions and rescheduling share conflict rules. Redis still handles verification codes, tokens and existing temporary locks, but is no longer the primary safeguard against duplicate occupancy in new bookings.

01 / ASYNC I/O
Asynchronous Entry
Tornado coroutines with asynchronous MySQL and Redis clients reduce thread blocking during I/O waits.
02 / COURT ROW LOCK
Shared Court Row Locks
Online, walk-in, rescheduling and maintenance transactions lock court rows before checking time ranges and active occupancy.
03 / IDEMPOTENCY
Idempotency & Constraints
Request keys, parameter hashes and stored results let identical retries reuse outcomes and reject changed parameters, protecting credits and redemption.
04 / EXPIRATION
Expiration & Recovery
Expired pending orders release court, stock or wallet holds. Critical state and ledger changes commit together or roll back.

The repository records a run through real Tornado HTTP routes with JWT and role checks: macOS arm64, Python 3.14.3, MySQL 5.7.28 and a pool limit of 10. Each scenario used one initial request followed by 200 requests with a concurrency cap of 20.

sections.title: From Continuous-Slot Recommendations to Quotes and Rescheduling
sections.body:
Reservation Lifecycle

Customers can select consecutive slots or supply an earliest start, duration and court preference to find fully available windows. Prefix sums identify contiguous openings; candidates are ranked by start-time deviation, preference, price and fragmented gaps. Up to three suggestions include reasons. A recommendation does not hold a slot: availability is checked again when booking.

Before confirmation, the quote shows list price, member discount, amount due and available balance, with stored value or project-internal simulated Alipay. Changed prices or benefits require reconfirmation; valid pending orders retain their agreed price snapshot. Cancellation, expiration and rescheduling handle resource release and price differences separately. Refunds return to the original payment channel, so simulated Alipay refunds do not credit the member wallet.

sections.title: A Membership Account Beyond Discount Labels
sections.body:
Membership & Community

The member center manages tier, expiry, balance, points and account history. Front-desk staff or administrators can process simulated top-ups, preserving the reason, operator and related business record. Pending holds are shown separately from available balance, allowing customers to reconcile top-ups, spending, refunds and manual adjustments rather than seeing only a balance.

Event registration, the player community, announcements, and notifications extend the platform across transactions, organization, and community engagement instead of limiting it to a booking tool.

sections.title: Payment Is Not the End: Make Collection Traceable
sections.body:
Club Commerce

Checkout rechecks price, stock and available balance and supports stored value and simulated Alipay. Pending orders reserve stock; successful payment creates a pickup QR code and readable code. Front-desk staff or administrators look up the order before confirming whole-order collection. Each order can be redeemed only once. A refund request freezes collection, and a completed refund invalidates the credential.

sections.title: Shared Business Records, Clearly Separated Roles
sections.body:
Front Desk & Roles

Front-desk staff open courts for unregistered walk-in customers at the full-slot list price. Arriving at 14:10 for 14:00–15:00 still incurs the full slot charge and ends at 15:00. Adjacent extensions, payments and operators remain traceable. Front-desk staff cannot publish events or announcements; maintenance staff only view reasons and scheduled windows, with reopening controlled by administrators.

sections.title: Explain Each Receipt, Not Just a Revenue Total
sections.body:
Reconciliation & Operations

The global ledger distinguishes channel receipts, top-ups, wallet spending and refunds, so a 100-yuan top-up followed by 100 yuan of wallet spending does not become 200 yuan of channel receipts. An ended booking is not proof of attendance: attendance rate and recording coverage are reported separately, and manual adjustments are kept out of operating receipts.

01
Concurrency-Safe Booking
Court row locks, transaction checks, idempotency and expiration protect business state.
02
Member Ledger
Top-ups, spending, refunds and manual adjustments retain their original business record and operator.
03
One-Time Pickup Redemption
Payment creates a credential for whole-order collection; refunds freeze pickup and repeated redemption is blocked.
04
Events and Community
Supports event registration, player content, announcements, and in-app notifications.
05
Operational Analytics
Separate booking rate, attendance rate and recording coverage instead of treating unknown attendance as absence.
06
Configurable Rules
Business hours, slot intervals, daily limits, and timeout policies are adjustable.

sections.title: One Content Loop for Creation, Review, and Reading
sections.body:
Overview

Moyu is not a single reading page. It is a web fiction business platform spanning content production, platform governance, and reader consumption. novel-app serves readers and authors, while ruoyi-ui provides the operations console. Both share the Spring Boot API and authorization model.

The platform organizes its workflow around books, chapters, drafts, bookshelves, subscriptions, comments, ratings, reports, reviews, and notifications, allowing each content change to continue into moderation, distribution, and feedback.

sections.title: From Discovering a Book to Following Every Update
sections.body:
Reader Journey

Readers discover content through recommendations, genres, rankings, search, and history before moving into book details and the reader. Bookshelves, subscriptions, reading progress, history, and notifications preserve continuity across sessions. Ratings, likes, comments, and reports feed reader signals back into governance.

sections.title: A Recoverable and Traceable Writing Workflow
sections.body:
Author Workflow

The author workspace covers profiles, works, covers, chapters, and drafts, including TXT and DOCX chapter import. The editor provides autosave, version history, and sensitive-content previews to reduce losses caused by interruptions, accidental edits, or unclear platform rules during long-form writing.

Submitted books and chapters enter explicit review states. Authors can track outcomes and notifications, while rejected content retains its reason and editing path to keep platform rules actionable.

sections.title: Risk Warnings First, Human Review for Final Decisions
sections.body:
Content Governance

The governance console supports book and chapter review, batch actions, rejection templates, sensitive-term context, risk ordering, and operational dashboards. Sensitive content follows a warning plus human review policy instead of automatic rejection. Dictionaries, allowlists, hit records, and review snapshots support each decision.

Report handling includes aggregation, content hiding and restoration, outcome notifications, and operation logs, turning reader feedback into an auditable governance loop.

sections.title: A Night-Reading Theme Across Discovery and Rankings
sections.body:
Product Experience

The interface uses dark night scenes, warm page tones, and physical book covers as primary visual signals, while keeping search, genre navigation, bookshelves, and creation entry points stable. The constellation ranking reinforces positions and titles visually without replacing familiar filters and list controls.

sections.title: Understanding through experimentation
sections.body:
These screenshots show actual runs using the site's built-in examples. The application currently uses a Chinese interface. Click an image to view it at full size.

01 / THE IDEA

When learning algorithms, reading pseudocode and explaining a particular decision can still feel like two different skills. I wanted an interface that connects them: predict an outcome, change a condition, then follow the execution to check your reasoning. Sorting, pathfinding and CPU scheduling give us three different things to observe: the order of numbers, a route across a map, and the time shared by tasks.

All three exhibits have the same four entry points: Learn, Run, Experiment and Compare. You can start with an explanation or go straight to the workbench. Pseudocode and the current step sit beside the visualization, with data and metrics below. Pause anywhere and you can connect the visible change to the operation behind it.

Explore Algorithm Museum↗

sections.title: Follow an element, not just a bar
sections.body:
02 / SORTING

The sorting workbench includes bubble, insertion, merge, quick and heap sort. Each element keeps its own ID, so even equal values remain distinguishable. Stability becomes something you can inspect: try 2, 1, 2, 1 and follow the equal elements through each step. Their changing positions give the definition something concrete to refer to.

Load sorted, reversed or duplicate-heavy arrays, or enter your own. Compare two or three algorithms on the same input and inspect comparisons, writes and modeled auxiliary space. Quick sort uses a fixed last-element pivot; I keep that choice explicit so its behavior on a particular input can be understood in context.

sections.title: Fewer steps can cost more
sections.body:
03 / PATHFINDING

In the pathfinding lab, you can draw walls, change cell weights and move the start and goal, then watch BFS, Dijkstra and A* explore. Give a shortcut a higher cost and the fewest steps may no longer produce the cheapest route. I want people to create that difference themselves and then revisit the conditions each algorithm relies on.

Ordinary BFS explains why it cannot run when the map does not have uniform edge costs. A separate negative-edge teaching example explicitly breaks Dijkstra's assumptions. The visualization shows exploration while the node table retains distances and predecessors. If there is no route, you can distinguish an unreachable goal from an input that the chosen algorithm cannot handle.

sections.title: Who runs first, and who waits?
sections.body:
04 / SCHEDULING

The CPU scheduler puts FCFS, SJF and round robin on the same timeline. Enter task arrival times and durations, then adjust the time slice and switching overhead to see how execution, waiting and idle time are distributed. What happens when a long task arrives first? How much switching overhead does a shorter time slice introduce? These are questions you can test directly.

The teaching model uses one CPU, no I/O and known task durations; SJF is non-preemptive. The ready queue and task data accompany the timeline, with response, waiting and turnaround times in the final results. I keep these simplifying assumptions visible so the conclusions stay tied to the model being explored.

sections.title: Keep the run, not just the result
sections.body:
05 / UNDER THE SURFACE

I separated computation, recording and playback. Algorithms execute in a Web Worker and produce events such as comparisons, swaps, node expansions and task switches. The interface reads those events to reconstruct state. Playback speed changes only the viewing pace; stepping back visits history, while running again with edited inputs creates a new experiment.

  1. 01 / COMPUTE

    Fix the conditions

    Record the input, seed, algorithm version and parameters before passing the work to a Worker.

  2. 02 / REPLAY

    Reconstruct from events

    Visuals, data tables, metrics and pseudocode all use the same execution record.

  3. 03 / KEEP

    Reopen an experiment

    Runs, comparisons and measurements live in IndexedDB and can be exported as backup files.

The interface uses React, TypeScript and Canvas 2D, with separate packages for the protocol, runtime, storage and each exhibit. I also distinguish operation counts from elapsed time on a particular device. Counts come from the execution record; timing comes from a separate series of repeated measurements. Those measurements include algorithm execution and event generation. Results below the timer's resolution are marked unreliable, and animation speed never serves as a performance ranking.

sections.title: Start by changing one condition
sections.body:
06 / TRY IT

All three exhibits are available in the browser without registration. On a first visit, I suggest choosing a familiar algorithm, running the default example and changing just one condition. Keep the original record and compare it with the new result. The difference is often easier to remember than another pass through the explanation.

Experiments stay in the current browser. Moving them to another device requires file export and import; accounts and cloud sync are not available yet. Full offline support is also planned, so the current version needs a connection to open. Next, I want to improve the counterexamples, teaching explanations and mobile controls so each experiment leaves you with a finding you can explain.

sections.title: Capture it, then keep reading
sections.body:
These six screenshots were captured on October 9, 2026, in WordNoteQA, an isolated demo build of the regular V1 interface. They use demo vocabulary and offline preset AI responses, not personal study records. They do not demonstrate live model quality or completed acceptance of newer features. The original windows and mixed English/Chinese UI text are preserved. Click an image to view the original.

01 / CAPTURE

Word Note began with a small frustration while moving between English-language courses, papers and technical reading. I would look up a word, understand it, and meet it again days later with only a vague memory of having checked it. Rather than start from a fixed vocabulary list, I wanted to keep the expressions I actually encountered and why they appeared on that page.

I kept the capture step light. The main window has room for a course, source and note; the menu bar opens a small floating panel. Enter the text, save it to the analysis queue and return to reading. An exact match for an English entry already in the notebook reuses its local meaning and brings it into the review queue, without another model request for the same word.

The input need not start in English. If I remember only the Chinese term for overfitting, I can use it to find the English expression. The result still enters the workflow as an English candidate. The previous result stays available while I type the next item, instead of keeping me in a waiting conversation.

sections.title: Let the meaning wait in Inbox
sections.body:
02 / CONFIRM

I do not let AI output go straight into the confirmed vocabulary. The original input, course and note stay in Inbox, beside the candidate's Chinese meaning, English definition, context and example. I check or edit it before saving. That pause matters for technical and ambiguous terms: a fluent explanation may not fit what I am reading.

I also keep the explanation requirements simple: explain the word itself first, and add a specialist meaning only when it is genuinely different. An ordinary word such as quick does not need an artificial AI context. If none of the candidates fits, I can create an entry manually. Failed analyses keep the original input for a later retry.

sections.title: Find it from the meaning you remember
sections.body:
03 / RETRIEVE

Keeping a term is useful only if I can find it again. Each entry retains its English headword, Chinese meaning, English definition and example, with the course and source alongside them. Vocabulary can be filtered by course and mastery, so returning to a class does not mean searching through every reading note.

Sometimes the spelling is exactly what I have forgotten. Search therefore covers Chinese meanings and handles both simplified and traditional characters. Searching for the Chinese meaning of quick brings the entry back. This is local text search, not another model guess, and it does not rewrite the saved text.

sections.title: Leave room to recall
sections.body:
04 / RECALL

The review screen hides the answer at first. I can start with terms due today or weaker terms, narrow the queue by course, then recall Chinese from English or English from Chinese. Recognizing an explanation on sight is not quite the same as retrieving it myself.

After revealing the answer, I choose Again, Hard, Good or Easy to schedule the next review. AI does not decide that I have mastered it. A term I want to leave for now can move to the end of the session or to tomorrow. This is the existing review flow; independent schedules for each direction and resumable sessions are still being validated in the newer version, not demonstrated by these screenshots.

sections.title: The engineering behind a small window
sections.body:
05 / NATIVE BY DESIGN

Most of the time, this tool should sit quietly beside my reading, so I chose native macOS. SwiftUI organizes the main interface, AppKit handles the floating panel and input completion, and SwiftData stores vocabulary and learning records. Appearance can follow the system or use a separate light or charcoal-dark theme, consistently across the main window and panel.

  1. 01 / INPUT

    Save the input first

    A new query becomes a local record before entering the analysis queue, rather than existing only inside a request.

  2. 02 / ANALYSIS

    Generate candidates

    Parse the structured response, validate the English entry and meaning, then send the candidates to Inbox for checking.

  3. 03 / VOCABULARY

    Confirm before learning

    Search and review use the confirmed vocabulary, stored separately from unconfirmed analysis results.

I separated queued analysis from the views, with one queue shared by the main window and floating panel. New input is saved first, one failed item does not block later items, and unfinished records can be recovered when the app reopens. Search, completion, lookup direction and review rules live in WordNoteCore. A replaceable AI client lets me check the workflow with preset responses instead of paid calls.

sections.title: Where it stands
sections.body:
06 / WHERE IT STANDS

Word Note is currently a local Mac application built from source, with no downloadable installer, accounts or cloud sync. Existing entries can be browsed, searched and reviewed offline. Generating new meanings requires a connection and your own DeepSeek API key; provider charges apply.

Local-first does not mean nothing leaves the device. When I request an analysis, that input and its relevant course name, source and note are sent to DeepSeek, but not the entire vocabulary as context. The key is kept in a permission-restricted local plaintext environment file, not an encrypted vault. I want those limits to be explicit rather than covered by a vague privacy promise.

Next, I care most about reliability over time: protecting manual edits during organization, making backup and restore previews clear, and continuing an interrupted review. These newer features have implementations and tests, but some integration and on-device acceptance checks remain. I want to settle those everyday details before expanding the scope.

projects.title: ML-SHARP
projects.lede: Turning one photograph into a scene with movable viewpoints

sections.title: Behind the photograph: a renderable set of 3D Gaussians
sections.body:
A street looking out to sea: vehicles in the foreground, buildings on either side, and water and a bridge in the distance. I fed the photograph into SHARP and moved the virtual camera slightly. The vehicles and distant scenery shifted by different amounts, giving the once-fixed street a sense of depth.

That subtle change is what drew me in. Without photographing the scene from every side or building a model by hand, a single image offers another way to see its spatial relationships.

I built a workflow around Apple's SHARP for single-image inference, 3D Gaussian export, viewpoint rendering and post-processing analysis. This showcase uses five scenes: a seaside street, coastal cliffs, architecture and trees, a chair by a window, and a campus corridor. I used the official model weights; my work focused on deployment, inspecting results and geometric post-processing, without retraining the base model.

SHARP predicts a 3D Gaussian representation from a single photograph, then renders nearby viewpoints. The movement in the videos comes from a virtual camera, not simply translating or scaling the original image.

Think of each Gaussian as a small colored ellipsoid in space, with a position, scale, orientation and opacity. During rendering, these ellipsoids are projected onto the image plane and composited according to occlusion. In the version used here, each scene contains two 768 × 768 layers, totaling 1,179,648 Gaussians in a PLY file of roughly 63 MiB.

This PLY is not a conventional triangle mesh. A Gaussian Splatting viewer can use it to show nearby viewpoints. For a blog, offline-rendered videos also let readers see the result without downloading an entire 3D scene.

There is an important limit: regions absent from the photograph have no direct observational evidence. My focus is parallax from small movements, not reconstructing a complete world for unrestricted exploration. This is also consistent with the SHARP paper's focus on nearby-view synthesis.

sections.title: Running the full workflow within 8GB of VRAM
sections.body:
Inference and rendering ran under WSL2 on Windows, using an RTX 3070 Laptop GPU with 8GB of VRAM. My Mac handled organizing the photos, collecting outputs and inspecting the results. The workflow follows these steps:

Input photo → Official FP32 inference → Gaussian PLY
                         ↓
                 Reload and validate
                         ↓
        Render with the official camera path
                         ↓
         Analyze and map post-processing edits

All five photographs shown here completed export, reload and moving-view rendering. The prediction stage took roughly 13–17 seconds, including input processing, the model forward pass and Gaussian post-processing. These are single-run observations on this device, not isolated model latency or a rigorous benchmark. VRAM usage approached the device's limit, so I processed images sequentially rather than in parallel.

I did not stop at a successful file write. Each PLY had to load again, pass checks on its decoded parameters, and actually render. One instructive detail was that the stored opacity field is a logit: fully opaque alpha = 1 corresponds to positive infinity. Rejecting every infinite value would incorrectly flag a valid result as corrupt. Validation needs to check the decoded opacity and other parameters, not just whether stored fields are finite.

The five scenes are a seaside street, coastal cliffs, architecture and trees, a chair by a window, and a campus corridor. Each offers something different to inspect: foreground-background parallax in the street, fine contours around trees and buildings, and occlusion and spatial structure indoors. The results preserve the main layout, though fine textures can become smoother and movement reveals issues less obvious in the original view.

Each scene pairs an input photograph with a two-second baseline video and an edit-location map. The videos use the official nearby-view trajectory to show SHARP's baseline parallax, without the post-processing described below. The maps separately record which Gaussians the post-processing changed.

sections.title: Two post-processing methods for two different problems
sections.body:
With parallax already visible in the baseline, I tried two post-processing methods that require no retraining. One adjusts local depth; the other removes low-contribution Gaussians. Each starts independently from the baseline rather than stacking the operations, so their effects remain distinguishable.

Correcting local depth along the camera ray

The first method targets isolated local depth anomalies. If the surrounding surface is fairly continuous but one Gaussian lies noticeably away from it, could I pull that point slightly toward the neighborhood's depth?

The difficulty is that real object boundaries also contain depth jumps. Branches, chair contours and foreground-background boundaries cannot simply be treated as insufficiently smooth. I inspect 5 × 5 neighborhoods of log depth in each Gaussian layer, using the median and a robust scale estimate to detect outliers while protecting image edges, genuine depth jumps and high-contribution regions. The model also predicts positional offsets, so adjacent grid entries need not be spatial neighbors; neighborhoods with excessive projection drift are skipped.

Selected points move along their original camera rays, by at most 3% per adjustment, while all three principal Gaussian scales change proportionally. In simplified form:

Position p' = r × p
Scale s' = r × s
0.97 ≤ r ≤ 1.03

This preserves the original-view projection center and approximate projected size without directly changing color or opacity. Depth changes can still affect occlusion, so I also protect the ordering between the two layers and render again to inspect the result.

This is a local anomaly correction. It cannot reconstruct unseen backsides or repair an entire incorrectly estimated surface.

Pruning Gaussians by multi-view contribution

The second method asks whether some of a scene's million-plus Gaussians contribute almost nothing within the viewing range being tested.

Taking inspiration from LightGaussian's multi-view importance-based pruning, I measure rendering contribution in the original view and several nearby views, then combine it with edge importance and opacity. The rules are my own experimental setup, not a reproduction of its full compression and recovery pipeline.

The contribution measurement uses a differentiable renderer. Temporary color channels are assigned to Gaussians, and gradients of the rendered output recover each point's alpha-compositing weight. Here, gradients are a counting mechanism, not model training. I take the maximum contribution across views rather than the average, to preserve points that become important from just one angle.

Only points with low contribution, away from important edges and meeting the opacity condition become pruning candidates. Each layer has a maximum removal budget of 10%. If fewer points qualify, fewer are removed rather than damaging structure to meet a quota.

sections.title: What the edit-location maps actually show
sections.body:
I fixed one condition when comparing the variants: the baseline, depth-corrected and pruned models use exactly the same camera intrinsics and extrinsics for every frame.

That matters more than it might seem. Regenerating a camera path from each variant's depth could make a model edit change the movement amplitude as well. Differences would then be hard to attribute to geometry rather than the camera.

Each edit-location map has four columns: depth correction in layer one, pruning in layer one, depth correction in layer two, and pruning in layer two. Red marks Gaussians whose depth was actually adjusted; cyan marks those removed. The layers belong to the model output, not before-and-after versions.

A map tells me where an algorithm acted. It is not an error heatmap or proof of how much was repaired. Marks follow the model's output grid, not the exact final projected positions. Removing one Gaussian does not mean removing the pixel at the same image location.

The five showcased scenes produced these results:

Post-processing measurements for the five scenes
SceneDepth editsPruned pointsPruned
Seaside street387,3147.40%
Coastal cliffs1413,1411.11%
Architecture and trees07,0860.60%
Window-side chair2931,2732.65%
Campus corridor068,1725.78%

Across these five scenes, only 46 Gaussians received a depth adjustment. No points in the architecture-and-trees or corridor scenes passed all the depth-correction conditions. Protecting edges and occlusions made this pass quite conservative. The street map has just three red marks but many more cyan ones; that difference in mark count does not translate directly into image-quality improvement.

The storage benefit of pruning is clearer. Removing about 7.40% of the street scene's points reduced its PLY from roughly 63 MiB to 58.34 MiB, while the tested nearby views stayed very close to the baseline. I did not measure playback frame rates after pruning, so fewer points cannot be reported as a demonstrated rendering speedup.

I did not observe a clear visual-quality improvement in this pass. High PSNR relative to the baseline only indicates a small change. Without measured depth or calibrated novel-view photographs, it cannot establish greater geometric accuracy. The baseline videos demonstrate the model's output, while the edit maps explain post-processing behavior; neither is evidence that post-processing improved the image.

The candidate statistics also showed that no layer reached its 10% budget: every eligible candidate had already been removed. The actual limit was therefore the filtering conditions, not the budget. Increasing an unused limit would not change the result. The next useful experiment is to inspect the protection conditions individually.

sections.title: Where I want to take it next
sections.body:
For now, the showcase keeps the five sets of input photographs, baseline videos and edit-location maps. Next, I want to choose a scene with a clear artifact, fix the camera path and relax one condition at a time, checking whether any gain justifies lost detail. External depth alignment is another possibility, but scale, focal length and coordinate conventions need to agree before another prediction can replace existing geometry.

For presentation, small interactive movements seem more appropriate than unrestricted navigation: a photograph could respond to the mouse or device orientation with controlled parallax. That is a future direction. The current showcase uses offline-rendered videos, not a real-time interactive viewer.

What I like about this project is the possibility of seeing a familiar photograph differently. Vehicles, buildings and distant water no longer pass through the frame at the same speed; depth emerges from that difference. What I want to refine next is how far the viewpoint can move while preserving the photograph's character and holding up from another angle.

projects.title: YOLO26 Multimodal
projects.lede: Multi-modal visual detection system based on YOLO26, featuring reusable Backbone and Neck architecture with three independent detection heads, outputting object detection, keypoint localization, and instance segmentation in a single forward pass.
images: Concept visualization from the original site

sections.title: One Model, Triple Perception
sections.body:
Overview

In real-world visual detection scenarios, we often need to simultaneously obtain an object's location (bounding box), shape (keypoints), and contour (segmentation mask). Traditional approaches typically require training a separate model for each task, then combining outputs via multi-model cascading or ensembling — adding system complexity and non-trivial inference latency.

The core idea of YOLO26 Multimodal is: leverage YOLO26's reusable Backbone and Neck to extract unified multi-scale features, then design three independent Detection Head, Keypoint Head, and Segmentation Head, each with its own loss function and output format. The entire system outputs all three result types in a single forward pass, achieving "one computation, triple perception."

sections.title: Multi-Head Architecture
sections.body:
Architecture

The architecture follows YOLO's One-Stage design philosophy with key innovations at the Head layer. While traditional YOLO Heads handle only single detection tasks (bounding box + class), we split the Head into three functionally independent branches, each with its own output channels, activation functions, and loss computation logic.

The key advantage is feature reuse — Backbone and Neck features are shared across three Heads, avoiding redundant computation. Each Head can be independently trained and fine-tuned without interference. When only one output type is needed, other Heads can be individually disabled for flexible capability trimming.

sections.title: A Reusable Feature Extraction Backbone
sections.body:
Backbone & Neck

YOLO26's Backbone is based on CSP (Cross Stage Partial) architecture, using CBS (Conv + BN + SiLU) modules as building blocks, with C2f modules for cross-stage feature fusion. The Neck uses PAN-FPN (Path Aggregation Network + Feature Pyramid Network) for bidirectional top-down and bottom-up feature aggregation.

Key design: We added a Channel Split mechanism at the Neck output, splitting the fused feature map along the channel dimension into three groups for the Detection, Keypoint, and Segmentation Heads. This lightweight separation is more efficient than feature map copying, adding only 0.3% parameters while effectively reducing gradient conflicts between tasks.

sections.title: Three-Head Design Details
sections.body:
Three Heads
📦
Detection Head
Handles object detection, outputting bounding box coordinates (x, y, w, h), objectness score, and class probabilities. Uses Decoupled Head design with independent classification and regression branches, CIoU Loss for localization. Anchor-free mode with direct center offset and dimension regression, supporting NMS post-processing.
🎯
Keypoint Head
Handles keypoint detection, outputting K predefined keypoint coordinates with visibility labels. Uses Heatmap-based approach generating H×W Gaussian heatmaps per keypoint, trained with MSE Loss. Supports variable keypoint counts (e.g., 17 for human body, 68 for face, 21 for hand) via flexible configuration.
🎭
Segmentation Head
Handles instance segmentation, generating pixel-level masks for each detected object. Uses Mask Prototype + Coefficients approach (similar to YOLACT), with a lightweight mask decoder requiring only 1ms. Outputs 128×128 mask prototypes, linearly combined via detection head coefficient vectors for final masks, balancing accuracy and speed.

sections.title: Multi-Task Loss Design
sections.body:
Loss Function

Each Head has its own loss function, with the total loss as a weighted sum:

L_total = λ₁ · L_det + λ₂ · L_kpt + λ₃ · L_seg

Where L_det includes CIoU localization loss, classification BCE loss, and objectness BCE loss; L_kpt uses keypoint heatmap MSE loss plus visibility classification loss; L_seg combines Dice Loss + BCE Loss for better foreground/background imbalance robustness.

Weight coefficients were determined through experimental tuning: λ₁=1.0, λ₂=0.5, λ₃=0.8. We also introduced dynamic weight adjustment — increasing L_det weight early in training for localization learning, then gradually raising L_kpt and L_seg weights for refined shape output.

sections.title: Training Strategy
sections.body:
Training Strategy

For the dataset, we collected and annotated approximately 12,000 images with multi-task labels, each containing bounding boxes, keypoint coordinates, and segmentation masks. Data augmentation uses Mosaic + MixUp + Random HSV + horizontal flip, with special geometric transforms for keypoints to ensure synchronized coordinate transformation.

Training uses AdamW optimizer with initial learning rate 1e-3 and cosine annealing schedule. Batch size is 32 (4×8 GPU) over 300 epochs. The first 50 epochs use Warmup + frozen Backbone, training only the Neck and three Heads to accelerate convergence and avoid early gradient oscillation.

sections.body:
Code

Multi-head inference forward pass flow

multimodal_infer.py
import torch
from yolo26 import YOLO26MultiHead

# Initialize multi-head model
model = YOLO26MultiHead(
    backbone='cspdarknet26',
    neck='pan_fpn',
    heads={'det': 80, 'kpt': 17, 'seg': 32},
    channel_split=True
)
model.load_state_dict(torch.load('yolo26_multi_best.pt'))
model.eval()

# Single forward pass → triple output
with torch.no_grad():
    det_out, kpt_out, seg_out = model(image)

# Detection: boxes + classes
boxes = det_out.boxes.xyxy    # [N, 4]
scores = det_out.scores       # [N, num_classes]

# Keypoints: [N, K, 3] (x, y, visibility)
keypoints = kpt_out.points

# Segmentation: [N, H, W] binary masks
masks = seg_out.masks

print(f"Det: {len(boxes)} | Kpt: {keypoints.shape[1]} pts | Mask: {masks.shape}")

sections.title: AI Gatekeeper for Metro Safety
sections.body:
Overview

Metro gate vaulting (or crawling under) is one of the most common violations in urban rail transit, causing both fare losses and serious safety hazards. Traditional approaches rely on manual monitoring, which is inefficient and prone to missed detections. This project uses a YOLOv5 object detection model trained specifically to identify gate vaulting behavior, deployed on a Rockchip RK3588 edge device for end-to-end real-time inference from video stream input to violation alerts.

sections.title: Scene Challenges
sections.body:
Challenge

Visual detection in metro gate scenarios faces multiple challenges:

  • Severe Occlusion — Narrow gate channels frequently occlude subjects via barriers and other passengers, requiring strong occlusion reasoning capability
  • Diverse Actions — Vaulting includes hurdle-style, hand-support, and crawl-under variants, lasting only 1-3 seconds, demanding high real-time detection performance
  • Complex Lighting — Underground platforms have variable lighting with backlighting, sidelighting, and fluorescent flicker
  • Edge Deployment — Must run on power-constrained embedded devices, requiring a sufficiently lightweight model

sections.title: Model Design
sections.body:
Model Design

Customized modifications based on the YOLOv5s architecture. First, we lightweight the Backbone by replacing standard convolutions in C3 modules with Depthwise Separable Convolutions, reducing parameters from 7.2M to 4.1M while maintaining feature extraction capability.

For the dataset, we collected 8,000+ frames from metro station surveillance videos, annotating three target classes: normal_pass, climb_over, and crawl_under. We used Mosaic + MixUp + random cropping augmentation, and introduced optical flow features from adjacent frames as auxiliary input to capture the temporal characteristics of vaulting actions.

sections.title: RK3588 Hardware Platform
sections.body:
Hardware

Rockchip RK3588 is one of the most powerful domestic edge AI SoCs, integrating quad-core Cortex-A76 + quad-core Cortex-A55 CPU, Mali-G610 GPU, and a dedicated 6 TOPS NPU (Neural Processing Unit). Its NPU supports INT8/INT16/FP16 mixed-precision inference, making it ideal for deploying quantized YOLO models.

Our development board features 8GB LPDDR5 memory and a dedicated NPU accelerator. Compared to GPU solutions (like Jetson Orin Nano), RK3588 offers lower power consumption (typically 5-8W vs 15W) and better cost-effectiveness, making it ideal for large-scale metro station deployments. The 6 TOPS NPU is more than sufficient for YOLOv5s-level models, achieving 60+ FPS in real-world testing.

sections.title: Deployment Pipeline
sections.body:
Deployment

Deploying from PyTorch model to RK3588 NPU requires the following key steps:

  • Step 1: Export ONNX — Export PyTorch model to ONNX format with fixed 640×640 input size
  • Step 2: RKNN Conversion — Use Rockchip's rknn-toolkit2 to convert ONNX model to RKNN format with INT8 quantization (500-image calibration set)
  • Step 3: NPU Deployment — Load RKNN model on RK3588 using rknn-lite2 runtime with NPU-accelerated inference
  • Step 4: Video Stream Integration — Capture RTSP video stream with OpenCV, feed frames to the model, and push results to the alert system via WebSocket

sections.title: Inference Optimization
sections.body:
Optimization

When deploying on RK3588, we performed multi-dimensional inference optimization:

  • INT8 Quantization — Using rknn-toolkit2 quantization, FP32 model is quantized to INT8, reducing model size 4x and improving inference speed 2.5x with only 1.2% mAP drop
  • Multi-core NPU Parallelism — RK3588 NPU supports 3-core parallel inference via core_mask=RKNN.NPU_CORE_0_1_2 for maximum throughput
  • Zero-copy Optimization — DMA buffer enables zero-copy transfer from video frames to NPU, reducing memory copy overhead
  • Async Pipeline — Video capture, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing run as an async pipeline to maximize throughput

rknn = RKNNLite()
rknn.load_rknn('yolov5s_gate.rknn')

articles.title: The Model Fits. Why Is It Still Slow?
articles.title_html: The Model Fits. Why Is It Still Slow?
articles.lede: KV compression saves memory and speeds up kernels. Why does the user see a different gain? Reading GAAC through bandwidth, concurrency, and measurement scope.
articles.author: Eric Pan
articles.body:
Memory capacity is usually the first obstacle when running a large language model locally. If BF16 weights will not fit, try 8-bit, then 4-bit. Once the weights finally load, it is tempting to think the hard part is over.

Yet generation can slow down again when we introduce long documents, a code repository, or several simultaneous tasks. The model has not run out of memory, and the GPU has substantial theoretical compute. Where is the time going?

Guo, George, and Joshi at Notre Dame offer a useful set of results in their October 28, 2026 preprint, GAAC: about 26% less resident KV memory, 1.19–1.27× faster attention kernels at 64K context on DGX Spark, 1.04–1.15× faster complete W4A16 decode steps, and 13%–29% higher aggregate throughput under fixed KV budgets.

Those figures describe different experiments. They do not combine into a claim that local models are now 20% faster. I want to use the paper to trace how saved capacity can, or cannot, become speed that a user actually experiences.

The weights fit. Historical tokens still need memory.

Weights are only part of the resident data used during inference. A Transformer also retains historical keys and values so that generating the next token does not require recomputing previous K and V states. This KV cache grows with context length and the number of concurrent sequences.

For a typical full-attention architecture, the theoretical storage for one sequence can be approximated as:

KV bytes = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim
           × context tokens × bytes per element

The initial 2 accounts for K and V. Consider 32 layers, 8 KV heads, a head dimension of 128, and BF16 storage: that is 128 KiB per token. At 65,536 tokens, one sequence needs 8 GiB; four equally long sequences without shared prefixes need 32 GiB for KV alone. This is an illustrative architecture, not a measured GAAC model, and excludes allocator overhead and temporary workspaces.

Weight quantization does not automatically shrink that cache. An 8B model has roughly 16 GB of raw BF16 weights or 4 GB at 4-bit, while its KV may remain BF16. Costs previously overshadowed by the weights become more prominent. GQA, MQA, sliding-window attention, and hybrid attention change that growth, so similarly sized models need not have similar KV requirements.

There is a less visible cost, too: caching avoids recomputation, not reading. In standard full attention, each new query still accesses historical keys and combines the corresponding values. Having room to store the data does not guarantee that each generation step can read it quickly enough.

That is why I would not evaluate the hardware using TFLOPS alone. Prefill can organize many input tokens into large matrix operations. Small-batch, single-request decode can repeatedly read weights and historical KV while leaving much of the arithmetic hardware underused.

As a bandwidth-floor example, suppose a path genuinely must read 8 GiB at an available decimal bandwidth of 1 TB/s. Transfer alone takes about 8.6 ms. This is not a GAAC kernel measurement and ignores cache hits and reuse. It simply illustrates the distance between “already in memory” and “free to access.”

Where does the compressed cache get unpacked?

FlashAttention already demonstrated the value of reorganizing computation and memory access. GAAC turns to the KV representation itself: if historical states are read repeatedly, can we move fewer bytes without changing the values stored?

BF16 consists of one sign bit, eight exponent bits, and seven mantissa bits. GAAC preserves the sign and mantissa and encodes only the exponent. Model-generated exponents are not uniformly distributed; frequently occurring exponents in many head-channels occupy short intervals. Calibration chooses high-coverage windows of length 8 and 16 for each head-channel of K and V in every layer. Encoding then stores offsets from those window bases.

Eight elements form a group sharing a 2-bit mode tag. If all elements fit the narrow window, the group uses 3-bit offsets; otherwise it tries 4-bit offsets. If any value still falls outside, the whole group falls back to raw 8-bit exponents. Outliers are not discarded. Poor calibration increases fallback and reduces compression efficiency rather than forcing an unrepresentable value into a short code.

In the common 3-bit mode, each element takes 8 + 3 + 2/8 = 11.25 bits. About 88%–90% of groups use that mode across the five models in the compression evaluation. Complete encoded-size ratios are 1.405–1.407×. A ratio of 1.406 means 1 - 1/1.406 ≈ 28.9% less encoded storage, not 40.6%. Once fixed slots, block tables, and fallback costs are included, resident KV savings are about 26%. That is not a 26% reduction in the entire model process.

Making KV smaller is not enough to make inference faster. A straightforward implementation reads the compressed data, decompresses the whole cache into device memory, and hands it to an ordinary attention kernel. That introduces a full-cache write followed by another read. The saved traffic can disappear in the unpacking process.

GAAC fuses reconstruction with attention. The kernel reads compressed tiles and metadata, reconstructs the BF16 values it currently needs, and immediately uses them for attention scores and weighted value sums. It never materializes a complete decompressed cache in external memory. New tokens first enter an incomplete BF16 tail block; a full block is compressed once, rather than repacked with every subsequent token. Blocks that exceed compressed-slot capacity remain in raw BF16.

I find these scheduling details as important as the codec. KV is not an archive file: it is appended, read, and released throughout inference. A compact representation may be a poor fit if every consumption requires an expensive detour. “Lossless” here means reconstructing the original KV bit patterns. It does not automatically make attention outputs or complete generated sequences bit-identical across different floating-point kernels. The integrated path still needs numerical validation.

More computation, less elapsed time

Table 5 breaks down a decode-attention kernel at 64K context. Times are in microseconds:

Component BF16 / FA2 Decompress first GAAC fused path
KV loading 1117.8 1117.8 823.5
Separate exponent decoding — 930.8 —
Computation, including GAAC reconstruction 241.5 241.5 290.7
Total 1359.3 2290.1 1114.2

GAAC spends 294.3 μs less loading KV and 49.2 μs more on computation, saving a net 245.1 μs. The speedup is about 1.22×, which means roughly 18% less elapsed time. Those are not two ways to say “22% less time.”

The decompress-first path takes 2290.1 μs, slower than the uncompressed baseline. The same compressed representation leads to opposite performance outcomes depending on where reconstruction happens and how the result is consumed.

Another ablation makes the tradeoff particularly clear. Adding a 2-bit mode improves the compression ratio from 1.406 to 1.439×, about 2.3%, but raises standalone decoding latency from 187.1 to 526.7 μs, around 2.8×. This is the Table 4 codec experiment, not the complete attention timing above. Still, a few more bytes saved do not necessarily pay for the extra cost of reading them.

I would therefore not treat reducing computation as the sole direction for optimization. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, some extra arithmetic can buy a larger reduction in memory traffic. How much arithmetic, where reconstruction happens in the memory hierarchy, and whether access remains regular all need to be measured together.

A 1.22× kernel does not make the request 1.22× faster

A decode step also includes linear layers, MLPs, normalization, weight access, and runtime overhead. Suppose attention originally consumes 40% of the total time and becomes 1.22× faster while everything else stays unchanged:

overall speedup = 1 / (0.6 + 0.4 / 1.22)
                ≈ 1.078

Overall processing rate improves by only about 7.8%. I chose 40% to illustrate Amdahl's law; it is not a measured fraction from the paper. The relevant question is how much of the original execution time belongs to the component being optimized.

GAAC's equal-batch experiment reflects that difference. Complete W4A16 decode steps on DGX Spark improve by 1.04–1.15×. In the two tested hybrid/MoE models, only about a quarter of the layers use full attention, and whole-step gains are around 1.04–1.06×. A faster attention kernel does not confer its percentage gain on every other layer.

The ranges also need their conditions attached. The 1.19–1.27× attention result uses batch 1 and 64K context on DGX Spark. The 1.04–1.15× complete-step range spans the tested models and context configurations. These are not a matched end-to-end pair that can simply be subtracted, and neither measures the completion time of a whole user request.

For a long document, prefill must process the input first. GAAC's fused path primarily accelerates decode; prefill retains conventional attention and may temporarily expand cached context when necessary. A 64K input followed by a few dozen generated tokens can spend most of its time before the first token. Generating thousands of tokens over that context offers more opportunity for per-step savings to accumulate.

The paper reports Qwen3-8B attention speedups of 1.31, 1.27, and 1.25× at 32K, 64K, and 128K. That is a useful warning against translating “long contexts expose memory costs” into “kernel speedup must rise monotonically with context.” Complete-step gains and kernel speedup ratios are different curves.

Higher total throughput is not faster output for each sequence

A separate experiment fixes the KV-memory budget and increases concurrency to the maximum each system can hold. In Table 2, Qwen3-8B with 64K context and about a 20 GB KV budget fits two BF16 sequences at 19.0 aggregate tok/s. GAAC fits three and produces 22.8 tok/s, a 20% increase.

Simple division gives about 9.5 tok/s per sequence for the first setup and 7.6 for the second. This is arithmetic on aggregate throughput, not a per-request latency measurement. It cannot establish an equal-batch slowdown because concurrency has changed. It does establish why aggregate throughput and per-sequence generation rate are not interchangeable metrics.

If the device serves one chat user, room for another sequence may offer no immediate benefit. If three tasks maintain separate long contexts, admitting all three instead of making the third wait could improve group completion time. That depends on scheduling and task dependencies. It is a hypothesis to test in deployment, not a multi-agent workflow experiment already performed by GAAC.

One contrast in the paper is especially revealing: the hybrid and MoE models show relatively modest equal-batch gains but 27% and 29% higher throughput under fixed KV budgets. Much of that benefit comes from accommodating another concurrent sequence, not from making each computation step faster by the same percentage.

An online service also needs queueing and tail-latency measurements. A larger batch can generate more tokens while keeping some requests waiting longer. I would define goodput against the product's requirements, for example counting only requests that meet both first-token and ongoing-generation latency targets. Real-time chat and offline document processing can have different constraints; one throughput ranking cannot select deployments for both.

What changes if the deployment already uses FP8?

Compression is not the only way to reduce KV costs. PagedAttention uses paged allocation and sharing to reduce fragmentation and duplication. Its paper reports 2–4× vLLM throughput against specific contemporary baselines and workloads, not a similar speedup for every matrix operation. GAAC additionally addresses the numerical representation and how attention consumes it.

FP8 halves the storage bit width relative to BF16 while introducing numerical approximation. In vLLM's April 2026 report, an H100 Llama-3.1-8B test with 150 requests, concurrency 8, and roughly 20K input/2K output tokens improves aggregate throughput from 450.3 to 517.5 tok/s, about 14.9%. The gpt-oss-20b variant that skips sliding-window layers gains about 4.8%. Different hardware and implementations prevent a ranking against GAAC, but halving bit width clearly does not imply doubling system speed.

Lossy paths also need task-accuracy and accumulation-error checks, not just matching cache sizes. GAAC itself achieves only 1.09–1.14× additional lossless compression on FP8 E4M3, and 1.25–1.30× on E5M2. These ratios further compress already quantized data. They neither restore BF16 precision nor establish the throughput gains measured with BF16 KV.

I would not conclude that either approach should replace the other. A deployment with mature FP8 kernels needs an incremental comparison. Preserving original BF16 KV values poses a different constraint and offers a different benefit. Hardware, architecture, precision, batch size, and workload need to be aligned before comparing results.

Losslessness leaves several deployment questions open

GAAC's exponent windows depend on calibration. In the positional-drift experiment in Appendix C, a Qwen3-8B layer uses windows calibrated on prompts of at most 8K tokens to process 32K input. Overflow storage for later keys grows substantially; 32K calibration is more stable. RoPE can shift key-exponent distributions with position. Reconstruction remains lossless, but compression efficiency and fallback overhead change.

This does not contradict cross-task calibration results. Windows selected on WikiText maintaining similar compression across several code, math, and knowledge tests do not establish coverage of every context length, content distribution, or long-running request trace. Deployment needs measurements of slot waste, fallback rates, prefix sharing, and cache turnover, not just one static cache's ratio.

Apple M4 results have a narrower scope, too. The authors implement compressed attention in Metal and compare it with a BF16-KV kernel of the same structure. At 64K context, they obtain about 1.10× for a single sequence and 1.25× for eight. This demonstrates kernel portability, not matching speedups for a complete Mac chat application or agent.

I would not infer energy efficiency either. The paper reports no power or energy measurements. The effect of extra computation and reduced traffic on temperature, battery life, and sustained performance needs separate testing. Lossless encoding, attention timing, complete-model quality, and whole-device energy use require distinct evidence.

The comparisons I would run before deployment

First, fix a reproducible baseline: model and quantization versions, inference framework and kernel, context and output lengths, KV precision, batch size, and request arrivals. Record weight memory, resident KV, and workspace separately. A reduction in one component is not the same percentage reduction in the entire process.

Then run two kinds of experiments. Hold concurrency fixed to compare complete decode-step and request latency. Separately, fix the memory budget and allow higher concurrency to compare aggregate throughput, queueing, and goodput. Both matter, but they should not be merged into a single “speed improvement” table.

Latency reporting needs its own distinctions. vLLM's metrics documentation separates time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and average time per output token (TPOT). State whether queueing is included, how observations are aggregated, and which output-token denominator is used. An average tokens/s can conceal both a short request's wait and a long request's stalls. P50/P95/P99, task quality, sustained memory use, and energy measurements bring the comparison closer to actual use.

For agents, I would also save task traces containing tool waits and repeated prefill. If a task spends most of its duration waiting for external tools, improving decode by 10% will not cut the whole task by 10%. Finding where the time goes determines which layer is worth optimizing next.

GAAC does not leave me with a universal speed promise. It makes me more interested in the denominator: encoded bytes or resident memory, one kernel or a complete step, single-user speed or concurrent capacity? Getting the model to fit is where these questions begin.

This discussion uses primary materials checked through November 3, 2026. GAAC figures refer to arXiv:2610.38210v1; I have not reproduced the experiments. The capacity calculation, Amdahl example, agent scenario, and proposed deployment comparisons are illustrations or engineering suggestions, not additional experimental results.
